337.title: Salutation to the Timeless
337.hook: namastvam akaale: salutation to the One beyond time (Jaap, bhujang prayat)
337.howItsDone: Sikhs greet one another with Sat Sri Akal, call God Akal Purakh, the Timeless Being, and recite namastvam akaale every morning in Jaap Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhujang prayat, the snake's gait, short, long, long, and your line, glide. Did something in your day move smoothly? Today, the first word of the glide. Day three hundred thirty-seven.

Look at your phone's lock screen. What's the biggest thing on it? On a lot of phones, it's the time. Not a photo, not a message. The hour and the minute, huge, in the middle. Calendars, deadlines, birthdays, the slow counting of years in a mirror. So much of a day is measured in time, and every clock is counting something down. Now listen to the first word Jaap Sahib salutes when it starts to glide. Today: salutation to the Timeless.
screen: `THE BIGGEST THING ON YOUR LOCK SCREEN.` → `THE HOUR AND THE MINUTE.` → `EVERY CLOCK COUNTING SOMETHING DOWN.`

segments.voice: The line is namastvam akaale. Namastvam is two words: namah, a bow, a salutation, and tvam, you. A bow to you. Akaale is the One who is akaal. Now open that word. Kaal is time. And in Punjabi and the older languages behind it, kaal also means death, because time is the thing that ends us. Put the small a in front, without, and akaal means without time, and without death. Timeless. Deathless. Both at once. So the very first salutation in the gliding part of Jaap bows to the One who isn't on the clock at all. Sikhs had met this word long before Jaap. In the Mool Mantar, the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak calls the One akaal moorat, the form beyond time. Sikhs call God Akal Purakh, the Timeless Being. In Amritsar, beside the Golden Temple, stands the Akal Takht, the Throne of the Timeless, which tradition says the sixth Guru, Guru Hargobind, founded. And the word is in the everyday Sikh greeting: Sat Sri Akal. Truth is the Timeless. A whole theology, folded into hello. Here's what it does on an ordinary day. Every person you love is in time. Your body is in time. Your worries are in time. Jaap's akaal points to something underneath all of it that isn't. Something the clock can't touch. Sikhs bow to that first, before anything else in the glide.
screen: `NAMASTVAM: A BOW TO YOU.` · `KAAL: TIME, AND DEATH.` · `AKAAL: TIMELESS, DEATHLESS.` · `SAT SRI AKAL: TRUTH IS THE TIMELESS.` · then, large: `BEYOND TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say namastvam akaale three times. Slowly, in the snake's rhythm from yesterday. Na-mas-tvam, a-kaa-le. Once. Twice. Three times. Then turn your phone face down, or put the clock out of sight, and sit in the quiet that's left. For these moments, don't count anything, not breaths, not seconds. Just be here, and let time be someone else's job. If you pray, you can rest in the word Akal. The bell holds the time.
Akaal. Without kaal, without time and without death: the Timeless One, the first salutation of Jaap's glide, and the Akal in Sat Sri Akal.
Your line: beyond time. Today, when you glance at the clock in a hurry, let it remind you: not everything is on the clock. Then take one slow breath. Day three hundred thirty-seven.

338.title: Salutation to the Merciful
338.hook: namastvam kripaale: salutation to the Merciful One (Jaap, bhujang prayat)
338.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of good things in daily life as kirpa, grace, often saying Waheguru di kirpa naal, by Waheguru's grace, and recite namastvam kripaale each morning in Jaap Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, akaal, the Timeless and Deathless, and your line, beyond time. Did a glance at the clock become a slow breath? Today, the very next line of the glide. Day three hundred thirty-eight.

A parking ticket, a library fine, a late assignment. You walk up ready to argue, already tired, and the person behind the counter looks at you, looks at the clock, and says: don't worry about it this time. That's it. No speech. Just a small door opening where you expected a wall. Moments like that tend to stay. Mercy has a way of doing that. And in Jaap Sahib, right after the bow to the One beyond time, comes a bow to exactly this. Today: salutation to the Merciful.
screen: `A FINE, A TICKET, A LATE ASSIGNMENT.` → `DON'T WORRY ABOUT IT THIS TIME.` → `A DOOR WHERE YOU EXPECTED A WALL.`

segments.voice: The line is namastvam kripaale. A bow to you, the Merciful. Kripaal comes from kirpa, or kripa: grace, kindness, mercy, favor you didn't earn. Kripaal is the One who is full of it. Now notice the order. The first line bowed to akaal, the Timeless, the One the clock can't touch. That could sound cold, a God too big and too far away to care about a parking ticket. So the very next line answers it. Timeless, yes. And merciful. In Jaap's order, the One beyond time is also the One who shows mercy. In Sikh teaching those two ideas belong together. Guru Nanak's hymns speak of nadar, the glance of grace, the kind look that lifts a person when their own effort has run out. Japji, which you walked through last year, says liberation comes through that grace. And the word kirpa is everywhere in Punjabi life, not just in prayer books. Ask a Sikh grandmother how the family is doing, and you may well hear: Waheguru di kirpa naal, theek haan. By Waheguru's grace, we're fine. A new job, a healthy baby, a safe journey, all described as kirpa. It's a way of saying: this wasn't only my doing. And it has a practical edge. Some Sikhs hear a question tucked inside the bow: if the One I salute every morning is merciful, where could I open a small door instead of a wall today? Jaap doesn't say that in so many words. It just puts mercy second in the glide, right after eternity.
screen: `KIRPA: GRACE, KINDNESS, MERCY.` · `TIMELESS, AND THEN MERCIFUL.` · `NADAR: THE GLANCE OF GRACE.` · `WAHEGURU DI KIRPA NAAL: BY GRACE.` · then, large: `SALUTE MERCY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one act of mercy for today. Think of someone who owes you something: an apology, an answer, a favor, a return of something borrowed. Or someone who's been a little careless with you lately. Picture their face. Breathe. And decide, quietly, to let one small thing go, the way the person at the counter did. Not everything. Just one. If you pray, you can say namastvam kripaale under your breath. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
Salutation to the Merciful. Namastvam kripaale: the second bow of Jaap's glide, to the One full of kirpa, grace and mercy.
Your line: salute mercy. Today, show mercy once: let one small debt, mistake or delay go, and say nothing about it. Day three hundred thirty-eight.

339.title: Formless, beyond compare
339.hook: arupe hain, anupe hain: without form, beyond comparison (Jaap, chachari)
339.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the short chachari lines of Jaap Sahib briskly each morning, and gurdwaras keep no images of God: the Guru Granth Sahib, a book of words, is the center.

segments.voice: Yesterday, salutation to the Merciful, namastvam kripaale, and your line, salute mercy. Did you let one small thing go? Today the rhythm changes again, and the lines get very short. Day three hundred thirty-nine.

Better than yesterday. Worse than her. Not as tall, as fast, as rich, as liked. Prettier than the old one. The mind is a measuring machine. It almost can't look at anything without setting it beside something else and checking which is bigger. A sunset gets compared to last week's. A child gets compared to a cousin. A few minutes of scrolling, and the comparisons pile up. And then a hymn says, in two words, that there is something nothing can be set beside. Today: formless, beyond compare.
screen: `BETTER THAN, WORSE THAN, NOT AS.` → `THE MIND IS A MEASURING MACHINE.` → `SOMETHING NOTHING CAN BE SET BESIDE.`

segments.voice: Further on, Jaap moves into a meter called chachari, and its lines are startlingly short. Each line is just two words. Aroop hain. Anoop hain. Ajoo hain. Abhoo hain. After the snake's long glide, it feels like quick footsteps, or a heartbeat. Hain means You are. So each line is a tiny sentence: You are this. Today, the first two, which the glide already saluted as aroope and anoope. Aroop: roop is form, shape, appearance, and the small a means without. You are formless. Nobody can paint You, sculpt You, put You on a screen. Sikhs take this seriously: there are no statues of God in a gurdwara, and the Guru Granth Sahib, a book of words, sits where you might expect an image. Then anoop. This one comes from upma, comparison, likeness. Anoop is the One with no likeness, nothing to compare to. And here the two words lean on each other. Comparison needs shapes. To say this is bigger than that, you need a this and a that, each with an outline. If the One has no form, there's nothing to measure against. Beyond compare isn't a boast that God wins every contest. It's that there's no contest at all. Now notice what that does for the measuring machine. Every morning, before the comparing starts, a Sikh reciting Jaap spends a few seconds saluting the one thing that can't be ranked. It's a small rest for the mind. A place where better than and worse than simply don't apply.
screen: `CHACHARI: TWO WORDS A LINE.` · `AROOP: WITHOUT FORM.` · `ANOOP: NOTHING TO COMPARE TO.` · `NO SHAPE, SO NO CONTEST.` · then, large: `BEYOND COMPARE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at something without comparing it. Pick one thing in front of you: a cup, a plant, your own hand, the sky in the window. Look at it for a while. Each time the mind says nicer than, older than, not as good as, notice it, smile at it, and come back to just this. This cup. This hand. Not better, not worse. Here. If you pray, you can say aroop hain, anoop hain softly. The bell holds the time.
Formless. Aroop hain, anoop hain: You are without form, and beyond compare, in the short, quick lines of Jaap's chachari meter.
Your line: beyond compare. Today, when you catch yourself measuring, someone else or yourself, stop at the word than, and leave the sentence unfinished. Day three hundred thirty-nine.

340.title: Unborn, beyond the elements
340.hook: ajoo hain, abhoo hain: never born, not made of earth or water (Jaap, chachari)
340.howItsDone: Sikhs say ajooni saibhang every day in the Mool Mantar at the start of Japji, and hear the same idea again in Jaap's ajoo hain, abhoo hain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, formless, aroop hain, anoop hain, and your line, beyond compare. Did you leave a comparison unfinished? Today, the next two short lines of the chachari. Day three hundred forty.

Everything you've ever touched was made of something. The table: wood, which was a tree, which was soil and rain and light. Your coffee: water, beans, heat. Your own body: about sixty percent water, plus minerals that were once in the ground, plus the air in your lungs right now. Even you had a birthday. A day, a place, a mother. Everything has a when it began and a what it's made of. Jaap Sahib names something that has neither. Today: unborn, beyond the elements.
screen: `THE TABLE WAS A TREE.` → `YOUR BODY: WATER, MINERALS, AIR.` → `EVERYTHING HAS A BIRTHDAY.`

segments.voice: The two-word lines keep coming. Ajoo hain. Abhoo hain. Start with the first. Joon is a Punjabi word for a birth, a life-form, a body you're born into. Ajoo, and its fuller form ajooni, means not born into any form. Never born. If that word sounds familiar, it should. It's in the Mool Mantar, Guru Nanak's words that open the Guru Granth Sahib, the lines many Sikhs learn first: ajooni saibhang, unborn, self-existent. Guru Arjan set them at the head of the scripture when he compiled it in 1604, and here the Tenth Guru brings the idea back, nearly two centuries after Guru Nanak, in his own morning praise. The first Guru and the tenth, saying the same thing in different meters. Then abhoo. Bhoo is the earth, the ground, the stuff things are made of. Abhoo: not made of earth. Sikh scripture often speaks of the body as made of five elements, earth, water, fire, air and space, borrowed for a while and given back. The One, Jaap says, isn't made of any of them. Not a very large person. Not a force inside the world like gravity. Something that isn't built from the world's materials at all. Sikh teaching holds firmly that the One is never born and never dies, and so is never shaped by any body. On an ordinary day, that matters. Everything you can touch will change, wear out, return to the ground, including your own hands. That can be frightening. Ajooni says that what you bow to is not on that list. Not made of this. Which means it can't wear out.
screen: `JOON: A BIRTH, A BODY.` · `AJOONI: NEVER BORN.` · `MOOL MANTAR: AJOONI SAIBHANG.` · `ABHOO: NOT MADE OF EARTH.` · then, large: `NOT MADE OF THIS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: touch earth and water, then be still. If you can, put your fingers on soil, a plant pot, a stone, or the floor. Feel it: solid, cool, made. Then touch water, a glass, the tap, a damp cloth. Feel it: wet, moving, made. Your hand is made of these too. Now take your hand away, rest it in your lap, and sit still. Let your attention go past what you can touch, to the quiet behind it. If you pray, you can say ajooni softly. The bell holds the time.
Ajooni. Never born into any body: the word from the Mool Mantar that Jaap echoes with ajoo hain, abhoo hain, unborn and not made of earth.
Your line: not made of this. Today, when something you own breaks or wears out, let it remind you: not everything wears out. Day three hundred forty.

341.title: Salutation to the armed One
341.hook: namo sastr paane: salutation to the One with weapons in hand, the protector (Jaap)
341.tomorrow: Sun of suns, moon of moons
341.howItsDone: Amritdhari Sikhs carry the kirpan as an article of faith tied to protecting others, and the Ardas said at the close of Sikh gatherings opens by remembering Bhagauti, the Divine as sword and power.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ajooni, never born, not made of earth or water, and your line, not made of this. Today Jaap does something surprising: after formless and unborn, it puts a weapon in the One's hand. Day three hundred forty-one.

A lifeguard's whistle. A crossing guard's raised hand and bright vest. A parent stepping, without thinking, between a child and a dog that's barking too hard. Protection doesn't always look gentle. Sometimes it's loud, and fast, and holding something. The lifeguard has a rescue tube. The guard has a stop sign. The people who stand between us and harm are rarely remembered as soft. They're remembered as there. Jaap Sahib has a line for the One who stands there. Today: salutation to the armed One.
screen: `A LIFEGUARD'S WHISTLE.` → `A PARENT STEPS BETWEEN.` → `PROTECTION ISN'T ALWAYS GENTLE.`

segments.voice: Among the salutations comes this one: namo sastr paane. Namo, a bow. Sastr, or shastar, is a weapon held in the hand, like a sword. Paan is the hand. Salutation to the One with weapons in hand. The next words add astr, a weapon that's thrown or shot, like an arrow: the One honored with that weapon too. It can be startling, right after aroop and ajooni, formless and unborn. Why would the formless need a sword? Because for the Tenth Guru, the sword is a picture of protection. He lived in violent years. His father, Guru Tegh Bahadur, was executed in Delhi. The Guru himself fought battles to defend his people, and in his Persian letter, the Zafarnama, he speaks of the four sons he lost. In that letter he wrote, in effect, that when every other way has failed, it is right to take up the sword. Not first. Last. So in Jaap the weapon in the One's hand isn't a threat to the innocent. It's the arm that defends them. That idea runs right through Sikh life. The Ardas, the prayer said at the close of Sikh gatherings, begins by remembering Bhagauti, a name for the Divine as sword and power. Amritdhari Sikhs carry the kirpan, a small sword, as an article of faith, a promise to protect, not a tool for picking fights. And the ideal has a name you met last year: sant sipahi, the saint-soldier. Gentle in the heart, ready in the hands. Jaap bows to the One who is both.
screen: `SASTR: A WEAPON HELD IN THE HAND.` · `WHY DOES THE FORMLESS NEED A SWORD?` · `ZAFARNAMA: THE SWORD COMES LAST.` · `SANT SIPAHI: THE SAINT-SOLDIER.` · then, large: `THE PROTECTOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of someone who protects you, or once did. A parent, a friend, a teacher, a nurse, a stranger who stepped in. Picture them clearly: their face, their hands, the moment they stood between you and harm. Breathe in, and remember what that safety was like. Breathe out, and thank them, silently. Then ask, gently: is there someone I stand between and harm? If you pray, you can say namo sastr paane. The bell holds the time.
Salutation to the armed One. Namo sastr paane: a bow to the One with weapons in hand, the protector who defends the weak.
screen: `SALUTATION TO THE ARMED ONE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the protector. Today, stand between someone and a small harm: a mean comment, a rushed decision, a forgotten bill. Be there. Day three hundred forty-one.

342.title: Sun of suns, moon of moons
342.hook: the Timeless is praised as the light within every light (Jaap)
342.tomorrow: Song of songs, dance of dances
342.howItsDone: Sikhs recite this doubled-word stanza near the end of Jaap Sahib each morning, and hear the same idea of one light in all at night in Kirtan Sohila.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the armed One, namo sastr paane, and your line, the protector. Did you stand between someone and a small harm? Today, Jaap looks up, at the sky. Day three hundred forty-two.

Here's a strange fact about the moon. It has no light of its own. Not a flicker. Every silver night you've ever walked under, every full moon over a parking lot or a lake, was sunlight, bounced. The moon is a mirror. And the sun? It's burning, yes, but it was formed too, out of something that came before it. Follow any light back far enough and you start to wonder where light itself comes from. Jaap Sahib asks that question with a single doubled word. Today: sun of suns, moon of moons.
screen: `THE MOON HAS NO LIGHT OF ITS OWN.` → `THE SUN WAS MADE TOO.` → `WHERE DOES LIGHT ITSELF COME FROM?`

segments.voice: Late in Jaap, the glide returns, and one stanza is built around doubled words. Namo soorj soorje: salutation to the sun of suns. Namo chandr chandre: to the moon of moons. Namo raaj raaje: king of kings. Namo indr indre: Indra of Indras. The pattern is the point. Sun of suns doesn't mean a bigger sun somewhere. It means the sun inside the sun, the light that makes the sun shine. Moon of moons: the brightness behind the reflected brightness. Whatever is greatest in its kind, the One is the source that makes it great. Then the stanza goes on, and here's the surprise. Namo andhkaare: salutation to the darkness. Namo tej teje: to the radiance of radiances. Darkness and radiance in one breath. In Jaap, the One is saluted in the night as well as in the bright things. And it ends: namo beej beeje, seed of seeds. The seed inside every seed, the start of every start. Sikhs hear a close idea in the evening too. In the prayer before sleep, Kirtan Sohila, Guru Nanak sings that one light is in everyone, and by that light all are lit. The Tenth Guru packs it into a doubled word; the first Guru gives it a whole hymn. Read this way, every bright thing you admire, a teacher's mind, a friend's laugh, a sky at dusk, is like the moon. Lovely, and lit from somewhere else. Jaap bows past the light to its source.
screen: `SOORJ SOORJE: SUN OF SUNS.` · `THE LIGHT INSIDE THE LIGHT.` · `DARKNESS AND RADIANCE, ONE BREATH.` · `BEEJ BEEJE: SEED OF SEEDS.` · then, large: `LIGHT OF LIGHTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a light source briefly. A lamp, a candle, a bright window. Never the sun itself. Look for just a moment, then close your eyes and watch the glow that stays behind your eyelids. Notice: even with your eyes shut, the light is still with you for a while. Then let it fade, and rest in the dark, which Jaap salutes too. If you pray, you can say namo soorj soorje softly. The bell holds the time.
Sun of suns. Namo soorj soorje: a bow to the light inside every light, the source that makes the sun shine and the moon glow.
Your line: light of lights. Today, when someone's brightness catches you, a smart idea, a warm laugh, enjoy it, and wonder for a second where it comes from. Day three hundred forty-two.

343.title: Song of songs, dance of dances
343.hook: salutation to the song within songs, the sound within sounds, the dance within dances (Jaap)
343.howItsDone: Music is central to Sikh worship: the Guru Granth Sahib is arranged by raag, and kirtan, singing its hymns with harmonium and tabla, fills the gurdwara; worship itself is sung rather than danced.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sun of suns, the light inside every light, and your line, light of lights. Today the same doubled pattern turns from what you see to what you hear. Day three hundred forty-three, the end of a week.

A backyard, late on a Saturday. Somebody puts on a song, an old one, the kind everybody's aunt knows. One person starts nodding. Then someone taps a spoon on the table. Then a grandfather who hasn't danced since the last wedding lifts one hand and turns his wrist, just once, and the whole room laughs and joins in. Nobody decided to dance. The song did it. There's something in music that moves people before they choose to move. Jaap Sahib salutes whatever that is. Today: song of songs, dance of dances.
screen: `A BACKYARD, A SONG EVERYONE KNOWS.` → `A GRANDFATHER TURNS HIS WRIST.` → `NOBODY DECIDED TO DANCE.`

segments.voice: Near the sun of suns, Jaap keeps doubling words, and now it reaches sound. Salutation to the song within songs. To naad naade, the sound within sounds. To the dance within dances. Same pattern as yesterday: not a better song, but the song inside every song, the thing that makes music move us at all. Naad is a word Sikhs know well. It means sound, and in Gurbani it often means the deep sound of the Divine, the music under everything, heard by the one who listens closely. Music isn't decoration in Sikh life. It's the main road. The Guru Granth Sahib is arranged by raag, by musical mode, so its hymns are grouped by the way they're meant to be sung. Sikh tradition remembers that Guru Nanak traveled with a musician, Bhai Mardana, who played the rabab while the Guru sang. Kirtan, singing the Guru's words, is at the heart of the gurdwara. Dance is different: worship in the gurdwara is sung, not danced. But Jaap isn't describing a ritual here. It's bowing to the movement in all moving things. The sway of a field of wheat. The turning of the seasons. The wrist of that grandfather in the backyard. And this is where the week ends. Seven days in Jaap: akaal, the Timeless; kripaal, the Merciful; aroop, formless and beyond compare; ajooni, unborn; the armed One, the protector; the sun of suns. And today, the song in every song.
screen: `THE SONG WITHIN SONGS.` · `NAAD: THE SOUND UNDER EVERYTHING.` · `THE GRANTH IS ARRANGED BY RAAG.` · `THE MOVEMENT IN ALL MOVING THINGS.` · then, large: `THE DANCE OF DANCES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: move to one song. Pick something you love, anything, a hymn, a shabad, a song from your childhood. Play it if you can, or hum it if you can't. Let one part of you move with it: a foot, a hand, a slow sway of the shoulders. Nobody's watching. Notice the moment the music starts moving you, rather than you moving to it. Then let the song end, and sit still with the quiet it leaves behind. The bell holds the time.
Song of songs. In Jaap's doubled salutations, a bow to the song within every song, the sound within sound, the dance within dance.
Your line: the dance of dances. Today, when music catches you, in a store, a car, a hallway, let yourself move a little, and notice what's moving you. Day three hundred forty-three. A week, done.

screen: `DAY 343 COUNTS.` → `A SECOND WEEK OF JAAP.` → `TOMORROW: LAMP OF BEAUTY.`
